question: If AI can solve math problems that people could not solve for years, how should we check its answers?
reflection: Machine-checked proofs could let people explore harder questions together, as long as humans still understand what has been proved.

sources.subject: OpenAI Astra solves 10 unsolved math proofs for $2,000 total

one_line: An unreleased model reportedly solved ten open math problems with proofs a computer can check, at a very low cost.

top_stories.title: AI solves open math problems
top_stories.what: OpenAI says its next model, Astra, solved ten long-open math problems and wrote each proof in a language that a computer can verify, for about 2,000 dollars of compute.
top_stories.why: Checkable results are a model for how AI findings in any field could be made trustworthy.

top_stories.title: Voice assistant that thinks while talking
top_stories.what: OpenAI rebuilt ChatGPT Voice so it can listen and speak at the same time and pass hard questions to a stronger model in the background.
top_stories.why: More natural voice talk could make AI interviews and phone surveys feel closer to human ones, which needs careful ethics.

top_stories.title: Training away feelings also hurts moral reasoning
top_stories.what: A reported Google study found that training a model to deny having inner experiences also weakened its moral judgement.
top_stories.why: Safety training can have side effects, so behaviour should be tested broadly after any change.

saudi_lens.text: Full-duplex voice in Arabic dialects would matter for Saudi customer services, but current reports do not say how well it handles them.

idea.title: Voice survey pilot with consent rules
idea.pitch: Test whether a natural-sounding AI voice changes answers in short phone surveys compared with a human caller, with clear disclosure.
idea.first_step: Draft a one-paragraph disclosure script and a five-question test survey.

idea_kids.title: Proof detectives
idea_kids.pitch: A puzzle book where children check each step of a simple number trick and mark the step that is wrong.
idea_kids.first_step: Write five short number tricks, each with one deliberate mistake.
